blocks.heading: Strategic, tactical and operational decisions
blocks.text: Strategic decisions set the long-term direction of the whole business and usually involve senior management and substantial commitment. Tactical decisions translate the strategy into departmental or medium-term action, often through middle management. Operational decisions organise routine day-to-day work, commonly through supervisors and lower-level managers. The difference concerns scope, importance and time horizon, not simply how difficult a decision feels. Opening a new region can be strategic, selecting a regional promotion plan tactical and assigning today’s delivery route operational. The decisions need alignment: efficient daily work cannot achieve a strategy if departments pursue incompatible targets. In a small enterprise one owner may make all three types, so do not assume different people are essential to the distinction. Escalate decisions beyond a role’s authority while allowing competent staff to handle appropriate routine matters.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tano Foods chooses to enter a new town next year. Its marketing head chooses a launch campaign, while a shift supervisor allocates today’s packing tasks. The market-entry choice is strategic; the campaign implementing it is tactical; the shift allocation is operational. A late packing task usually needs an operational response first, unless it reveals a persistent problem requiring a wider change.

blocks.heading: Strategic decisions
blocks.text: Strategic decisions concern the long-term direction and major objectives of the business. They are normally taken at senior level and can commit substantial resources, such as entering a new market or changing the main product range. Their effects spread across functions and cannot be assessed from today’s work schedule alone.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Yeta Tools decides whether to establish operations in another region. This changes direction and long-term commitment, so it is strategic. The subsequent daily dispatch choices implement the strategy but are not themselves the same decision.

blocks.heading: Tactical decisions
blocks.text: Tactical decisions turn wider strategy into more specific plans, often for a department or a medium-term period. They concern how to implement the strategic direction, for example a promotion programme or departmental capacity plan. Middle managers commonly make them within agreed authority. A small owner may also make tactical decisions; classification follows the decision’s scope rather than the title alone.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Elo Foods has chosen to enter a new town and its sales head chooses a three-month launch campaign. The campaign is tactical because it implements the market-entry strategy. It differs from both choosing the new market and allocating a worker’s task today.

blocks.heading: Operational decisions
blocks.text: Operational decisions concern routine day-to-day activity, such as allocating shifts, scheduling a delivery or reordering ordinary supplies within an agreed plan. Supervisors and lower managers often make them. They still affect customers and costs, but their scope is narrower than the business’s strategic direction. Escalate an unusual commitment beyond the role’s authority instead of treating every daily problem as permission to change strategy.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Onda Works’ supervisor assigns today’s available staff to existing orders. This is operational because it implements current commitments. Choosing a completely new product market would require a wider strategic decision.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Coordinated management and decision levels
blocks.text:
Hela Packs misses its weekly dispatch target. Existing capacity is sufficient, but materials and staff are scheduled at different times. A supervisor can introduce a coordinated rota and daily checks within existing authority. The owner is considering buying a second production line as an alternative. For part (b) only, an independent capacity assessment now shows that even fully coordinated use of the existing line cannot meet continuing contracted demand. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate the two responses to Hela’s missed target under the original facts. Explain the managerial decision levels involved. [12]
b Evaluate the responses after the capacity assessment changes. Explain whether the original judgement should change. [12]

a Coordinating the existing rota is operational and fits the stated mismatch; planning, allocation, guidance and review make it a complete management response. Buying a second production line is a strategic investment decision for senior management, because it commits substantial finance to long-term capacity. Because capacity is sufficient, start with coordination rather than expansion. Daily checks should assess completed dispatches rather than an unrelated intermediate-output count. The decision is conditional on the stated adequate capacity. b The assessment removes that condition: even efficient coordination cannot meet continuing contracted demand. Keep the rota because poor coordination would still waste resources, but it is no longer sufficient. Senior management should now evaluate extra capacity, including a second line, against cost, resources and contract durability. The judgement changes towards investigating investment rather than relying on the operational fix alone. Do not buy automatically; the capacity case is now stronger, but affordability and implementation remain to be assessed.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Coordinated management and decision levels
blocks.text:
Nawa Desks misses a delivery target because cutting and assembly schedules do not match. Existing equipment and staff are adequate when work is coordinated. The supervisor proposes a shared daily schedule and progress checks. The owner instead considers a new factory without first investigating the mismatch.

a Explain how effective management could improve Nawa’s ability to meet its delivery objective. [8]
b Evaluate whether the missed target should trigger an operational correction or an immediate strategic expansion. [12]

a Planning should translate the delivery promise into a workable sequence; organising should allocate cutting and assembly staff and materials consistently. Leading should clarify priorities and enable staff to report difficulties. Controlling should compare progress with the agreed schedule and investigate differences. The functions reinforce one another: checks provide information for revised allocations, while clear guidance makes the revised plan understandable. Since capacity is stated to be adequate, coordination can reduce unfinished work and protect customer confidence without assuming extra machines are necessary. b Operational correction is narrower and can target the known scheduling failure. It preserves resources while testing whether the existing setup can fulfil commitments. Strategic expansion might support future growth, but that need is not established and it adds a long-term cost before the actual cause is resolved. Choose the coordinated schedule and review delivery completion. Escalate to tactical capacity planning or strategic investment only if reliable evidence shows a wider constraint. Effective management means selecting a response suited to the cause and level, not making the most expensive decision.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Coordinated management and decision levels
blocks.text:
Nawa Desks misses a delivery target because cutting and assembly schedules do not match. Existing equipment and staff are adequate when work is coordinated. The supervisor proposes a shared daily schedule and progress checks. The owner instead considers a new factory without first investigating the mismatch.

a(i) Define effective management. [2]
a(ii) State two features of strategic decisions. [2]
b State two connected activities in effective management after an objective has been set. [2]
c Explain why Nawa needs coordinated cutting and assembly schedules to meet its delivery target. [6]
d Evaluate the supervisor’s operational response compared with the owner’s proposed new factory. [8]

a(i) Planning, organising, leading and controlling people to achieve business objectives and solve problems. a(ii) They set long-term direction and usually involve senior-level commitments affecting the whole business. b Allocating tasks and resources, and comparing actual progress with the target. c The customer needs complete desks, so cutting and assembly must deliver compatible components at the right time. Coordination directs existing staff and equipment towards the promised result rather than accumulating unfinished parts. Progress checks can reveal delays while action is still possible. d A shared schedule addresses the stated cause with existing adequate capacity and lies at operational level. A new factory is a strategic commitment that could add cost without correcting the mismatch. Start with the supervisor’s response and review results. Reconsider larger investment if evidence later shows a persistent capacity shortage rather than assuming every missed target requires expansion.
